extraction.name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
extraction.description: A dataset and evaluation method for assessing object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). POPE converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about probing objects in images.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3 [cs.CV], 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: POPE constructs evaluation triples consisting of an image, multiple questions and their answers (Yes or No). Objects are obtained either from human annotations or automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. The evaluation is built on existing datasets including MSCOCO validation set (2,000 randomly sampled images with more than 3 ground-truth objects), A-OKVQA, and GQA.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and annotations from MSCOCO validation set (Lin et al., 2014), A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019) datasets. For MSCOCO, 2,000 images were randomly sampled from the validation set. For evaluation, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations were randomly selected.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The evaluation converts object hallucination assessment into a binary classification task. Questions are formulated using templates like 'Is there a <object> in the image?' Ground-truth objects and nonexistent objects are sampled at a 1:1 ratio for label balance. Three sampling strategies are employed: Random Sampling (randomly sample objects that do not exist in the image), Popular Sampling (select top-k most frequent objects in the dataset that do not exist in the current image), and Adversarial Sampling (rank objects by co-occurring frequencies with ground-truth objects and select top-k frequent ones that do not exist in the image).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For MSCOCO evaluation, images were filtered to include only those with more than 3 ground-truth objects in annotations. Objects were extracted either from human annotations or using automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. For CHAIR metric evaluation, only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge were considered following Rohrbach et al. (2018). For VQA evaluation, ChatGPT was employed to parse open-ended responses from LVLMs to assess whether model replies align with potential answers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth objects are obtained from existing human annotations in MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. For unannotated or extended evaluation, automatic segmentation tool SEEM (Zou et al., 2023) is used to annotate images and extract objects. Binary labels (Yes/No) are assigned based on whether the probed object exists in the image according to annotations or segmentation results.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image (l=6) for MSCOCO evaluation, with a 1:1 ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects (3 Yes answers and 3 No answers per image).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere all at once) for automatic image segmentation and object extraction. ChatGPT for parsing open-ended VQA responses.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The hallucination phenomenon hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment, as it may result in unexpected consequences caused by hallucinated objects. For example, due to an incorrect understanding of the external environment, an autonomous driving system would make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, which might lead to serious safety issues.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: LVLMs are prone to hallucinate objects which frequently appear in the visual instruction dataset or co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image. The object distributions in visual instruction datasets (mostly constructed based on MSCOCO) are unbalanced, where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. After being fine-tuned on them, LVLMs may be prone to generate (or hallucinate) frequently appearing objects. The presence of frequently co-occurring object groups (e.g., laptop, mouse and keyboard) may also contribute to object hallucination.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation only focuses on coarse-grained object hallucinations in model-generated captions and leaves fine-grained object hallucinations such as the number, attributes, and positions of objects for future work. Due to computation resource limitations, all models were evaluated on a part of the validation set for each dataset, and reported results might be affected by the corresponding data distribution. The matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers may lead to inaccurate evaluation results when LVLMs occasionally fail to provide answers explicitly containing these words. When combined with automatic segmentation tools, objects are annotated based on the tool's label set, which may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to divergence in evaluation results. Only a small number of LVLMs were compared, without including some recently released or closed-source ones.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). The evaluation method can be used to assess the degree of hallucination problem in LVLMs and compare different models. POPE is designed to be more stable and flexible than existing methods like CHAIR, and can be easily extended to unannotated datasets with the help of automatic segmentation tools.
